title: Constantine (312–313)
hookLine: the emperor's victory, the Edict of Milan, and a freedom that brought new temptations

cards: Two Christian writers of the emperor's own time tell the same story, and they don't tell it the same way. Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the throne.
Lactantius says he was told in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did.
Eusebius, writing later, says Constantine told him, and swore to it, that he saw a sign of light in the sky, a cross above the sun, with words: by this, conquer. Either way, he wins.
And the world of the persecuted Church turns upside down.

teach.b: First, the sign. It's honest to say the sources differ: a dream in one, a vision in the sky and then a dream in the other.
What they agree on is that Constantine put a Christian sign on his army, and credited his victory to Christ. Second, the letter.
Afterward, Constantine and his fellow emperor Licinius agree on a policy, and Lactantius copies the letter that announces it.

teach.h: FREEDOM FOR CHRISTIANS AND ALL OTHERS.
teach.b: It grants to Christians, and to all others, the free choice to follow whatever worship each person wants. Church buildings and property taken in the persecution are to be given back. People call it the Edict of Milan.
Remember Nicomedia, and the books burning in the market square. Now Christians can ask for their churches back. Third, the surprise.
Freedom was a gift, and it came with new temptations. The emperor gave the church money, buildings and favor. Bishops found themselves near the throne.
Being Christian became useful for a career. Eusebius himself, who admired Constantine, complains in his Life of Constantine about hypocrites who slipped into the Church to win the emperor's goodwill.
And Constantine, Eusebius says, was baptized only near the end of his life. Fourth, why it matters now. Persecution asks one question: will you stay?
Comfort asks a quieter one: why are you here?
The Church after Constantine had to learn to answer the second question.

how: In Catholic tellings of Church history, Constantine's reign marks the end of the great persecution and the start of the Church's public life in the empire, with new freedom and new temptations.

games.q: you're Constantine, after the victory, agreeing a policy with Licinius. what does your letter grant?
o: freedom of worship for Christians only.
free choice of worship for Christians and all others.
an order that everyone become Christian.
games.why: the letter Lactantius copies grants free choice to Christians and to all others, and orders church property returned.

practice: Think back to a stretch of your life when things were hard, then one when things were easy, and notice where your attention was in each: on God, on the people you love, on what matters most.
Don't judge it; just notice what changed. Then look at today: is anything comfortable crowding out something that matters? If you pray, bring that to God honestly.

wordCard.voice: Constantine. The emperor who won under a Christian sign, granted freedom of worship, and brought the Church both peace and new temptations. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: by this, conquer — the words Eusebius says came with the sign. In Latin: in hoc signo vinces.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom, and its dangers. Tomorrow, the emperor's mother takes the road east. Day seven hundred sixteen, done.
